title: Facade and glazing risk screening
audience: Trainee or new worker on the window cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Identify safety and authorisation decisions associated with facade and glazing risk screening.
Explain the applicable risk hierarchy and specialist responsibilities for facade and glazing risk screening.
Produce a defensible stop-work, competent-person referral or restricted handover using mock evidence.

instruction.heading: Where this lesson sits
instruction.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level work, water-fed pole work and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Work above ground level, or work from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted. It needs written authorisation from the employer under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson is a desk-based drill. It does not give permission to work at height, on a roof, from a platform, or on a solar system. Safe Work Australia's working-heights page sets the high-risk construction threshold at a fall of more than 2 metres. In NSW, a safe work method statement is needed where a person could fall more than 2 metres. South Australia lowered its high-risk construction threshold from 3 metres to 2 metres, effective 1 July 2026. Check the rule in your own state or territory before any real work.

instruction.heading: What facade screening is for
instruction.body: Facade and glazing screening is the step where you look at the exterior and separate three things: what you can see, what you cannot see, and who has to decide the rest. It is not an engineering assessment. A worker can record what is visible, such as a crack in a pane, a gap in a sealant line, a loose fixing, a stain that suggests water, or debris on a ledge. Those are observations. A conclusion that a panel is secure, or that an overhead element will stay in place, is an inference, and it needs a building specialist to confirm it. Approval to work is a third thing. It comes in writing from the person who controls the site and the work. Keep the three apart in every record. The point of this lesson is that a visible sign does not tell you the engineered condition, and that missing information becomes an open decision, never a permission.

instruction.heading: Applying the risk hierarchy to a facade
instruction.body: Safe Work Australia's risk-management code ranks controls from most to least effective. The top levels are to eliminate the hazard, to substitute it or isolate people from it, and to use engineering controls. The lowest level is administrative controls and personal protective equipment, which depend on people behaving correctly. On a facade, eliminating the hazard means taking the elevated work out of scope, so the worker does not go up to look. Isolation means keeping people out of the area beneath a damaged element and marking the boundary. Engineering controls, such as a barrier or a catch zone, are designed by a specialist and are not improvised by a cleaner. Administrative controls include the permit, the signage, the briefing and supervision. Personal protective equipment comes last. A hard hat beneath a cracked overhang does not make the overhang safe, and it does not change the restriction.

instruction.heading: Information needed before any work is allocated
instruction.body: Before anything is allocated, confirm five things. These are the work order and its exact scope; the name and contact details of the site controller; the current method approval for the work, if one exists; the location-specific risk assessment; and the licence or authorisation status of any equipment that would be used. Also confirm access, the exposure of pedestrians and neighbouring premises, the weather, and whether the building owner or managing agent has been told about any damage. Where any item is missing, record it as an open decision. An open decision means the affected work does not go ahead until a person with authority closes it in writing. It is never treated as silent permission.

instruction.heading: The lesson case: cracked glazing under an overhead element
instruction.body: The lesson case is a photograph of cracked glazing beneath an overhead facade element, taken after building maintenance. Start from the restriction. The overhead element, and any work near it, is out of scope until a building specialist has assessed it. Do not infer that the panel is structurally sound because it looks intact in the photograph, or because the building is in use. A photograph cannot show the fixing, the load path, or the condition of the element above the glass. The first safe action is to stop and keep people out of the area beneath the element. Tell the site controller and the building contact, record the time and the names of the people told, and request a specialist assessment. Do not remove the cracked glass, do not climb, and do not tell the client that the area is safe. A separate, ground-level scope that sits clear of the overhead element may continue only if the site controller confirms it in writing and the area is isolated from the cracked element.

instruction.heading: Role boundaries and the stop-work decision
instruction.body: General cleaning training does not sign off rope descent, platform operation, anchor certification, electrical clearance or emergency rescue capability. A trainee who finds that one of these is needed must refer it, not attempt it. Structural assessment of a facade belongs to an appropriate building specialist, and electrical assessment belongs to a licensed electrician. The stop-work rule applies whenever the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; when wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions; when exposed wiring, damaged cable or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected; when a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; when the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or when you are asked to work above ground level without the required licence or authorisation. When the rule applies, stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming.

instruction.heading: Records and communication
instruction.body: Use dated records to show the exact observation, the source document, the person notified, the time, the restriction applied, and the response requested. Describe what was seen in plain words, and label each statement as an observation, an inference or an approval. Keep each entry short. Do not write safe, certified or compliant unless the evidence and the authority both support the word. The record is what protects the people who read it later, including the client and the next worker on the site.

instruction.heading: Licence and height rules differ by jurisdiction
instruction.body: The licence picture is set by each state and territory, so check the rule where you work. For a boom-type elevating work platform, the WP licence applies to a boom of 11 metres or more in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. The Queensland definition places platforms shorter than 11 metres outside its scope. The Victorian WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code uses the same 11-metre threshold, measured from the original design, and expects operators of shorter booms to be trained. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria, and the Northern Territory expects the operator to be competent. Window-cleaning licence status by state: NSW: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; VIC: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; QLD: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; WA: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; SA: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; TAS: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; NT: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04; ACT: no licence required under the official state page checked 2026-11-04. Pressure-cleaning, roof soft-washing and solar-panel-cleaning licence status: UNCONFIRMED.

instruction.heading: Electrical notice
instruction.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. The NSW definition of electrical wiring work includes installing, repairing, altering, removing or adding to an installation, and it also covers supervising that work. Victorian rules on PV installation, on whether PV DC cables stay live when the system is switched off, and on PV panel cleaning could not be read in this pass. As general practice, treat all panels, cables and exposed wiring as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instruction.heading: Trainer-led tabletop practice
instruction.body: Work through the case using fictitious work orders, drawn plans, photographs of a mock facade and blank record sheets. Annotate a mock facade map with the defects you have observed, the points that are unknown, and the people who must be notified. The trainer checks each entry for accuracy and stops any proposal to carry out unauthorised work on a real building.

procedure: Read the fictitious work order, and confirm in writing which parts of the scope are above ground level.
Mark any element above ground level as excluded, and record that the restriction applies.
Record each visible sign as an observation, with its location, time and photograph reference.
Record any conclusion about soundness or stability as an inference, and mark it for specialist assessment.
Isolate the area beneath any damaged or uncertain element, and keep people out of it.
Notify the site controller and the building contact, and record who was told, how, and when.
Apply the stop-work rule if any trigger is present, and record the stop.
Write the restricted handover: completed scope, excluded elevations, referrals and open decisions, with no safety or compliance claim the evidence does not support.

workedExamples.situation: A photograph shows cracked glazing beneath an overhead facade element after building maintenance. The work order asks for the whole frontage to be cleaned.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop, and keep people out of the area beneath the element. Treat the element and the work near it as out of scope until a building specialist has assessed it. Tell the site controller and the building contact, and record the time and the names. Do not infer soundness from the photograph. Request a specialist assessment in writing and record the request. Do not remove the cracked glass or climb to look at it.

workedExamples.situation: A damaged glass panel is noted at ground level while inspecting the exterior cleaning scope. The panel is not under any overhead element.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the ground-level panel be cleaned, and who decides?
workedExamples.reasoning: The panel is clear of the overhead element, so the question becomes one of scope. Record the panel as an observation, with its location and photograph, and do not state that it is safe or unsafe. Tell the site controller and ask for a written decision before any work near it. Keep the area isolated, and do not disturb the damaged edge of the glass while waiting for the decision.

workedExamples.situation: The owner asks for the upper windows to be cleaned today, because the weather is fine and a ladder is already on site.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the work above ground level. The restriction needs written employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and any required licence. A ladder on site is not an authorisation. Record the request, the time and the response, and tell the supervisor. Offer to record the upper windows as excluded in the handover, with the reason.

equipmentAndPpe: Fictitious work order, site controller contact card and method approval extract (desk materials only).
Mock facade map and drawn elevation with numbered zones.
Photograph cards of cracked glazing, staining and loose fixings, using training or fictitious images.
Observation, inference and approval record sheet.
Stop-work card and restricted handover template.
For any future real site, PPE and access equipment are set by the site controller and the risk assessment. No access equipment or PPE is used in this desk-based lesson.

commonErrors.error: Treating a photograph as proof that a panel or element is sound.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the photograph as an observation, and refer the structural question to a building specialist.

commonErrors.error: Treating an intact appearance as evidence of a secure fixing.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep observation and inference in separate entries.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a verbal go-ahead from the maintenance crew.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask for the approval in writing from the site controller, and record it.

commonErrors.error: Leaving the area beneath a cracked element open to people.
commonErrors.prevention: Isolate and mark the area, and tell the site controller at once.

commonErrors.error: Starting work at height because the equipment is already on site.
commonErrors.prevention: Equipment on site is not authorisation. Check the restriction, the licence and the written approval first.

commonErrors.error: Writing safe or certified in a record.
commonErrors.prevention: Use observed-only wording, and list what was not inspected.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and height notice. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on roofs, from elevated work platforms, or on solar systems. Completing it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. The jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction boom-length and class rules are set out in the instruction above and in the references. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. Check your state or territory rule and obtain written employer authorisation before any work above ground level.

Falls and scaffolds. Safe Work Australia's working-heights page places the high-risk construction threshold at more than 2 metres. SafeWork NSW describes a hierarchy in which fall prevention comes first, work positioning second, and fall-arrest systems only as a last resort, with a risk assessment and worker consultation before any control is chosen. A worker who is not licensed for scaffolding must not erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold where a fall could exceed 4 metres, according to the same NSW page.

Stop-work rule. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

Electrical notice. This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. The NSW definition of electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering an installation. Victorian PV rules could not be read in this pass. Treat all panels, cables and exposed wiring as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

Risk hierarchy. Safe Work Australia's risk-management code places administrative controls and personal protective equipment at the lowest level, and treats them as a last resort or a back-up (copy dated December 2011, section 4.1; a later edition was not read).

qualityStandard: Visible signs are separated from engineered confirmation, and open unknowns are recorded with the person responsible.
The area beneath any cracked or uncertain element is isolated, and the building specialist is named as the referral.
Structural soundness is not inferred from a photograph, and no safety or compliance claim is made that the evidence does not support.
The stop-work rule is applied and recorded where a trigger is present.
Trainer-led practice uses only photographs, drawn plans and fictitious work orders.
documentationEvidence: Observation, inference and approval record for each element, with time and source.
Notification record showing who was told, how, and when.
Stop-work note where a trigger applies.
Restricted handover listing the completed scope, excluded elevations, referrals and open decisions.
summary: Facade and glazing condition is screened from what is observed, and a photograph is never treated as proof of structural soundness.
Cracked or uncertain glazing and overhead elements are isolated and referred to an appropriate building specialist.
This is a desk-based drill on invented job sheets, and it permits no raised or elevated task.

knowledgeChecks.question: For facade and glazing risk screening, what evidence must be established before allocating work, and which facts are still unverified?
options: Structural soundness inferred from a photograph of the facade, the frame, the glass and the panels taken from the street by the crew today
The work order, site controller details and method approval, with visible signs distinguished from engineered confirmation and open unknowns recorded
A cracked panel assumed to be cosmetic because the building is in use by tenants, visitors and the public at all hours of the day and night
The building maintenance crew's word that the glazing is sound, was checked last month by the team, and needs no further review at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker sees cracked glazing beneath an overhead facade element. What is the first safe action?
options: Remove the cracked glass so the area is clear for the work to proceed today
Isolate the area beneath the element, keep people out, and tell the site controller
Carry on with the ground-level cleaning and mention the crack in the final report
